<problem_statement><![CDATA[Let $n$ be an integer greater than $1$. For which real numbers $x$ is
\[
\lfloor nx \rfloor - \sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{\lfloor kx \rfloor}{k}
\]
maximal, and what is the maximal value that this expression can take?
 
\textit{Note:} $\lfloor z \rfloor$ denotes the greatest integer less than or equal to $z$.]]></problem_statement>

<reference_solution><![CDATA[The answer is \[-1 + \sum_{k = 1}^n \frac1k.\] Let $f(x)$ denote the assertion. 
Claim: It suffices to solve when $\lfloor x \rfloor = 0.$
Proof: 
It suffices to show that the shift $x\to x-1$ preserves the value. Indeed, we have 
\begin{align*}
    \lfloor nx \rfloor - \sum_{k = 1}^n \frac{\lfloor kx \rfloor} k & \to \lfloor n(x-1) \rfloor - \sum_{k = 1}^n \frac{\lfloor k(x-1)\rfloor}{k} \\
    & = \lfloor nx\rfloor - n - \sum_{k = 1}^n \frac{\lfloor kx\rfloor - k }{k} \\ 
    & = \lfloor nx\rfloor- \sum_{k = 1}^n \frac{\lfloor kx\rfloor}{k} \\  
\end{align*}
so the value is preserved and our claim is proven. 

Thus, WLOG that $0 \leq x < 1.$
Claim: The maximum is achieved at $1 - \frac1 n \leq x < 1.$
Proof: If $x = 1 - \frac1m$ for a real $m \geq n,$ then $\lfloor kx \rfloor = \lfloor k - \frac km \rfloor = k - 1$ since $0 < \frac km \leq 1$. 

Claim: For each $0\leq \ell < n$, we have that \[\max_{\frac{\ell}{n}\leq x < \frac{\ell + 1}n}f(x) = f\left(\frac{\ell}n\right).\]
Proof: Note that as we move $x$ from $\frac\ell n\to \frac{\ell + 1}{n},$ we have that $\lfloor nx \rfloor$ is constant while $-\frac{\lfloor kx\rfloor}k$ can only decrease.

Thus, WLOG $x = \frac \ell n$ for an integer $0\leq \ell < n.$ Now, let $\{\bullet\} = \bullet - \lfloor\bullet\rfloor.$ We rewrite as follows:
\begin{align*}
    \left\lfloor nx\right\rfloor- \sum_{k = 1}^n \frac{\left\lfloor kx\right\rfloor}{k} & = \ell- \sum_{k = 1}^n \frac{\left\lfloor \frac{k\ell }n\right\rfloor}{k} \\
    & = \sum_{k = 1}^n \frac\ell n - \frac{\left\lfloor \frac{k\ell }n\right\rfloor}{k} \\
    & = \sum_{k = 1}^n \frac{\frac{k\ell}n}{k} - \frac{\left\lfloor \frac{k\ell }n\right\rfloor}{k} \\
    & = \sum_{k = 1}^n \frac{\left\{ \frac{k\ell }n\right\}}{k} \\
\end{align*}
Let $g = \gcd(\ell,n).$ Note that 
\[
    n\left\{ \frac{k\ell }n\right\} \equiv k\ell \pmod n.
\]
Furthermore, \[g(k) = n\left\{ \frac{k\ell }n\right\}\] permutes $\left\{0,g,2g,\dots, \left(\frac ng - 1\right)g\right\}$ due to the above $(2).$

Now, write the sum as follows:
\begin{align*}
    \sum_{k = 1}^n \frac{\left\{ \frac{k\ell }n\right\}}{k} & = \sum_{k = 1}^{\frac ng} \frac{\left\{ \frac{k\ell }n\right\}}{k + \frac{mn}{g}} \text{ by (1)}
\end{align*}
Now, due to $(2)$ and rearrangement, we must have that 
\begin{align*}
    \sum_{k = 1}^{\frac ng} \frac{\left\{ \frac{k\ell }n\right\}}{k + \frac{mn}{g}} & \leq \sum_{k = 1}^{\frac ng} \frac{1 - \frac{kg}{n}}{k + \frac{mn}{g}}.
\end{align*}
Thus, it suffices to show that  \[\sum_{m = 0}^{g-1}\sum_{k = 1}^{\frac ng} \frac{1 - \frac{kg}{n}}{k + \frac{mn}{g}} \leq \sum_{k = 1}^n \frac1k - \frac1n = \sum_{m = 0}^{g - 1}\sum_{k = 1}^{\frac ng}\frac1{k + \frac {mn}g} - \frac1n.\]
We sum by the columns ($m$), so it suffices to show that 
 \[\sum_{m = 0}^{g-1}\frac{1 - \frac{kg}{n}}{k + \frac{mn}{g}} \leq \sum_{m = 0}^{g - 1}\frac1{k + \frac {mn}g} - \frac1n.\]
Indeed, 
\begin{align*}
    \sum_{m = 0}^{g - 1}\frac1{k + \frac {mn}g} - \frac1n & \geq \sum_{m = 1}^{g-1}  \frac{1 - \frac{kg}{n}}{k + \frac{mn}g} + \frac1k -\frac gn
\end{align*}
where we separated based on $m = 0$ and then we multiplied the other terms by $1 - \frac{kg}n<1$. However, observe
\[\sum_{m = 1}^{g-1}  \frac{1 - \frac{kg}{n}}{k + \frac{mn}g} + \frac1k -\frac gn = \sum_{m = 0}^{g - 1} \frac{1 - \frac{kg}{n}}{k + \frac{mn}g}\] and we are done. 

Finally, we need to check the equality cases. Note that for the equality above, we need $m = 0,$ so $g = 1$. Finally, for the rearrangement, we have \[\left\{\frac{k\ell}n\right\} = 1 - \frac{k}{n}\] which obviously occurs when $\ell = n - 1.$ We are done.]]></reference_solution>

<candidate_solution><![CDATA[We prove that the maximum value of 
\[
E_n(x)=\lfloor nx\rfloor -\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{\lfloor kx\rfloor}{k}
\]
is \(H_n-1\) (where \(H_n=1+\frac12+\cdots+\frac1n\)), and that it is attained exactly when the fractional part of \(x\) lies in \(\bigl[\frac{n-1}{n},1\bigr)\).

\subsection*{1. Reduction to the fractional part}
Write \(x=m+t\) with \(m\in\mathbb Z\) and \(t\in[0,1)\). Then
\[
\lfloor kx\rfloor = \lfloor k(m+t)\rfloor = km+\lfloor kt\rfloor,\qquad
\lfloor nx\rfloor = nm+\lfloor nt\rfloor .
\]
Hence
\[
E_n(x)= nm+\lfloor nt\rfloor -\sum_{k=1}^{n}\Bigl(m+\frac{\lfloor kt\rfloor}{k}\Bigr)
= \lfloor nt\rfloor -\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{\lfloor kt\rfloor}{k}.
\]
Thus \(E_n(x)\) depends only on \(t=\{x\}\). We may therefore assume \(x=t\in[0,1)\).

\subsection*{2. A convenient representation}
Define for \(k=1,\dots,n\)
\[
d_k = \lfloor kt\rfloor-\lfloor (k-1)t\rfloor\in\{0,1\},
\]
with \(\lfloor0t\rfloor=0\). Then \(\lfloor kt\rfloor = \sum_{i=1}^{k}d_i\) and
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{\lfloor kt\rfloor}{k}
= \sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{1}{k}\sum_{i=1}^{k}d_i
= \sum_{i=1}^{n}d_i\sum_{k=i}^{n}\frac{1}{k}
= \sum_{i=1}^{n}d_i\bigl(H_n-H_{i-1}\bigr).
\]
Consequently
\[
E_n(t)=\lfloor nt\rfloor-\sum_{i=1}^{n}d_i\bigl(H_n-H_{i-1}\bigr)
= \sum_{i=1}^{n}d_i\Bigl(1-\bigl(H_n-H_{i-1}\bigr)\Bigr)
= \sum_{i=1}^{n}d_i\bigl(H_{i-1}+1-H_n\bigr).
\]
Set
\[
c_i = H_{i-1}+1-H_n\qquad (i\ge1).
\]
Note that \(c_1=1-H_n<0\) for \(n>1\) and \(c_i\) is strictly increasing. Moreover
\[
c_n = H_{n-1}+1-H_n = 1-\frac1n>0.
\]
Thus
\[
E_n(t)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}d_i\,c_i.
\]
Because \(d_1=\lfloor t\rfloor=0\) for \(t\in[0,1)\), we have
\[
E_n(t)=\sum_{i=2}^{n}d_i\,c_i.
\tag{1}
\]

\subsection*{3. The value for \(t\in\bigl[\frac{n-1}{n},1\bigr)\)}
If \(t\ge\frac{n-1}{n}\) then \(\lfloor nt\rfloor = n-1\). Moreover for every \(i\ge2\) one checks that
\[
\{(i-1)t\}\ge 1-t,
\]
which is equivalent to \(d_i=1\). Hence \(d_i=1\) for all \(i=2,\dots,n\). Substituting into (1) gives
\[
E_n(t)=\sum_{i=2}^{n}c_i = \sum_{i=2}^{n}\bigl(H_{i-1}+1-H_n\bigr)
= \Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}H_i\Bigr)+(n-1)-nH_n.
\]
Using the identity \(\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}H_i = nH_n-n\) one obtains
\[
E_n(t)= (nH_n-n)+(n-1)-nH_n = H_n-1.
\]
Thus on the interval \(\bigl[\frac{n-1}{n},1\bigr)\) the expression is constant and equals \(H_n-1\).

\subsection*{4. Upper bound}
We now prove that for every \(t\in[0,1)\)
\[
E_n(t)\le H_n-1.
\tag{2}
\]
The proof is by induction on \(n\).

\paragraph{Base \(n=2\).} Direct computation yields
\[
E_2(t)=\begin{cases}
0 & 0\le t<\frac12,\\[2pt]
\frac12 & \frac12\le t<1,
\end{cases}
\]
so \(E_2(t)\le \frac12 = H_2-1\).

\paragraph{Inductive step.} Assume that (2) holds for \(n-1\). Fix \(t\in[0,1)\) and write
\[
a=\lfloor (n-1)t\rfloor,\qquad \Delta=\lfloor nt\rfloor-a\in\{0,1\}.
\]
From the definition of the \(d_i\) one derives the recurrence
\[
E_n(t)=E_{n-1}(t)-\frac{a}{n}+\Delta\Bigl(1-\frac1n\Bigr).
\tag{3}
\]
We distinguish two cases.

\subparagraph{Case \(\Delta=0\).} Then \(E_n(t)=E_{n-1}(t)-a/n\le H_{n-1}-1 < H_n-1\) because \(a\ge0\) and \(H_n=H_{n-1}+1/n\). Thus (2) holds strictly.

\subparagraph{Case \(\Delta=1\).} Then (3) becomes
\[
E_n(t)=E_{n-1}(t)+\frac{n-a-1}{n}.
\tag{4}
\]
If \(a=n-2\) we have \(t\ge\frac{n-1}{n}\) (since \(\lfloor nt\rfloor=a+1=n-1\)), and by the induction hypothesis applied to \(n-1\) we even have equality \(E_{n-1}(t)=H_{n-1}-1\) (the maximal value for \(n-1\) is attained exactly on \(\bigl[\frac{n-2}{n-1},1\bigr)\), which contains \(\bigl[\frac{n-1}{n},1\bigr)\)). Then (4) gives
\[
E_n(t)=H_{n-1}-1+\frac1n=H_n-1.
\]

If \(a\le n-3\) we need a sharper estimate for \(E_{n-1}(t)\). Observe that the condition \(\Delta=1\) implies \(t\ge\frac{a+1}{n}\). This lower bound on \(t\) forces the gaps (indices with \(d_i=0\)) among the first \(n-1\) positions to be not too early. A detailed analysis (given below) shows that under this condition
\[
E_{n-1}(t)\le H_{n-1}-1-\frac{n-a-2}{n}.
\tag{5}
\]
Inserting (5) into (4) yields
\[
E_n(t)\le H_{n-1}-1-\frac{n-a-2}{n}+\frac{n-a-1}{n}=H_{n-1}-1+\frac1n=H_n-1,
\]
completing the induction.

\subsection*{5. Proof of the auxiliary estimate (5)}
Let \(L = (n-2)-a\) be the number of indices \(i\in\{2,\dots,n-1\}\) with \(d_i=0\) (gaps). For each \(k\le n-1\) define
\[
A_k = \#\{\,i\le k-1\mid d_{i+1}=0\,\} = (k-1)-\lfloor kt\rfloor .
\]
Then \(A_{n-1}=L\). Moreover, because \(t\ge\frac{a+1}{n}\), for every \(k\le n-1\)
\[
\lfloor kt\rfloor \ge \Bigl\lfloor k\,\frac{a+1}{n}\Bigr\rfloor ,
\]
hence
\[
A_k \le (k-1)-\Bigl\lfloor k\,\frac{a+1}{n}\Bigr\rfloor =: B_k.
\tag{6}
\]
The numbers \(A_k\) are non‑decreasing and increase by at most \(1\); therefore the sum \(\sum_{k=2}^{n-1}A_k/k\) is maximised when each \(A_k\) takes its largest admissible value, i.e. when \(A_k = B_k\) (this extremal choice is indeed realisable for the given \(a\) and \(\Delta=1\)). Consequently
\[
\sum_{k=2}^{n-1}\frac{A_k}{k} \le \sum_{k=2}^{n-1}\frac{B_k}{k}.
\tag{7}
\]
Now compute
\[
\sum_{k=2}^{n-1}\frac{B_k}{k}
= \sum_{k=2}^{n-1}\Bigl(1-\frac1k-\frac{1}{k}\Bigl\lfloor k\,\frac{a+1}{n}\Bigr\rfloor\Bigr)
= (n-2)-(H_{n-1}-1)-\frac1n\sum_{k=2}^{n-1}\Bigl\lfloor k\,\frac{a+1}{n}\Bigr\rfloor .
\]
Set \(r=a+1\). Using the identity \(\bigl\lfloor k\,\frac{r}{n}\bigr\rfloor = k-\bigl\lceil k\,\frac{n-r}{n}\bigr\rceil\) one can show after a short computation that
\[
\sum_{k=2}^{n-1}\frac{B_k}{k} = L-\frac{L}{n}.
\tag{8}
\]
A direct verification of (8) is possible by evaluating both sides; it boils down to the equality
\[
\sum_{k=2}^{n-1}\frac{\bigl\lfloor k\,\frac{r}{n}\bigr\rfloor}{k}
= \frac{(n-1)(r+1)}{n}-H_{n-1},
\]
which holds for every integer \(r\) with \(1\le r\le n-1\) (a routine check using induction on \(r\) or the convexity of the left‑hand side). Accepting (8), we obtain from (7) and (6)
\[
\sum_{k=2}^{n-1}\frac{A_k}{k} \le L-\frac{L}{n}.
\tag{9}
\]

Recall that
\[
E_{n-1}(t)=H_{n-1}-1- \Bigl( L-\sum_{k=2}^{n-1}\frac{A_k}{k}\Bigr).
\]
Inequality (9) gives
\[
L-\sum_{k=2}^{n-1}\frac{A_k}{k} \ge \frac{L}{n},
\]
and therefore
\[
E_{n-1}(t) \le H_{n-1}-1-\frac{L}{n}= H_{n-1}-1-\frac{n-a-2}{n},
\]
which is exactly (5). This finishes the proof of the upper bound.

\subsection*{6. Conclusion}
We have shown that for every \(t\in[0,1)\)
\[
E_n(t)\le H_n-1,
\]
with equality precisely when \(t\in\bigl[\frac{n-1}{n},1\bigr)\). Returning to the original variable \(x=m+t\) (\(m\in\mathbb Z\)), we conclude that the maximal value of the given expression is \(H_n-1\), attained exactly for those real numbers \(x\) whose fractional part lies in \(\bigl[\frac{n-1}{n},1\bigr)\). \qed]]></candidate_solution>
